subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Principal Values
stem: The principal solution of \(\cos^{- 1}\left( - \frac{1}{2} \right)\) is
solution:
**(C)**

The principal value of \(\cos^{-1}x\) lies in \([0,\ \pi]\).

Let \(\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \theta\), so \(\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) with \(\theta \in [0,\ \pi]\).

We know \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), and \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\), so
\(\cos\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), i.e. \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Since \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \in [0,\ \pi]\), it is the required value.

\(\therefore \cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

(Option D, \(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), is outside the principal branch and in any case \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = 0\); options A and B give \(+\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).)

stem: Find the general solution of \(cosx - sinx = 1.\)
solution:
We have \(\cos x - \sin x = 1\).

Divide throughout by \(\sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{2}\):

\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cos x - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(\therefore \cos x\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \sin x\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(\therefore \cos\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

The general solution of \(\cos\theta = \cos\alpha\) is \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha\), \(n \in Z\).

\(\therefore x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

\(\therefore x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2n\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) or \(x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2n\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)

\(\therefore x = 2n\pi\) or \(x = 2n\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), where \(n \in Z\), is the required general solution.

Check: \(x = 0\) gives \(1 - 0 = 1\); \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) gives \(0 - (-1) = 1\). Both satisfy the equation.

stem: If \(\sin^{- 1}(1 - x) - 2\sin^{- 1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) then \(x\) is
solution:
**(C)**

Let \(\sin^{-1}x = \alpha\), so \(x = \sin\alpha\). The given equation becomes

\(\sin^{-1}(1 - x) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\alpha\).

Taking sine of both sides:

\(1 - x = \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\alpha\right) = \cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha = 1 - 2x^{2}\).

\(\therefore 1 - x = 1 - 2x^{2}\)

\(\therefore 2x^{2} - x = 0\)

\(\therefore x(2x - 1) = 0\), so \(x = 0\) or \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Taking sine can introduce extra roots, so both must be tested in the original equation:

- \(x = 0\): \(\sin^{-1}(1) - 2\sin^{-1}(0) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Valid.
- \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 2\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \neq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Rejected.

\(\therefore x = 0\).

stem: Find the general solution of \(sinx + sin3x + sin5x = 0\).
solution:
We have \(\sin x + \sin 3x + \sin 5x = 0\).

Group the first and last terms (they are the ones equidistant from \(3x\)) and use \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\):

\(\therefore (\sin x + \sin 5x) + \sin 3x = 0\)

\(\therefore 2\sin 3x\cos 2x + \sin 3x = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 3x\,(2\cos 2x + 1) = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 3x = 0\) or \(\cos 2x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore \sin 3x = 0\) or \(\cos 2x = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

The general solution of \(\sin\theta = 0\) is \(\theta = n\pi\), and of \(\cos\theta = \cos\alpha\) is \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha\), \(n \in Z\).

\(\therefore 3x = n\pi\) or \(2x = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

\(\therefore x = \dfrac{n\pi}{3}\) or \(x = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), where \(n \in Z\), is the required general solution.

Check: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) gives \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \sin\pi + \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 0 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0\).

stem: Show that \(\cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{4}{5} \right) + \cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{12}{13} \right) = \cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{33}{65} \right)\).
solution:
Let \(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right) = \theta\). Then \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}\) and, since \(\dfrac{4}{5} > 0\), \(0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - \cos^{2}\theta} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{16}{25}} = \dfrac{3}{5}\)  (positive, as \(\theta\) is in the first quadrant).

Let \(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = \phi\). Then \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{12}{13}\) and \(0 < \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore \sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{144}{169}} = \dfrac{5}{13}\).

Now \(\cos(\theta + \phi) = \cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi = \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) = \dfrac{48}{65} - \dfrac{15}{65} = \dfrac{33}{65}\)  ...(1)

Also \(0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(0 < \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(0 < \theta + \phi < \pi\), which is the principal branch of \(\cos^{-1}\).

\(\therefore\) from (1), \(\theta + \phi = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{33}{65}\right)\).

\(\therefore \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{33}{65}\right)\). Hence shown.

stem: The principal solutions of \(secx = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\) are
solution:
**(B)**

\(\sec x = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\ \Rightarrow\ \cos x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)

Principal solutions are the solutions that lie in \([0,\ 2\pi)\).

Here \(\cos x > 0\), so \(x\) lies in the first or the fourth quadrant, and the reference angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) because \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

First quadrant: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\)

Fourth quadrant: \(x = 2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\)

Check the second value: \(\cos\dfrac{11\pi}{6} = \cos\left(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(\sec\dfrac{11\pi}{6} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\). Both values satisfy the equation.

Hence the principal solutions are \(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) — option (B).

Why the others fail: \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2 \neq \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\), which rules out (A); and \(\dfrac{11\pi}{4} = 2.75\pi\) is greater than \(2\pi\), so it is not a principal solution at all, which rules out (C) and (D).

stem: Prove that: \(\sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{3}{5} \right) + \cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{12}{13} \right) = \sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{56}{65} \right)\).
solution:
Let \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \theta\). Then \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}\) and, as \(\dfrac{3}{5} > 0\), \(0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore \cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}\).

Let \(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = \phi\). Then \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{12}{13}\) and \(0 < \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore \sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{144}{169}} = \dfrac{5}{13}\).

Now \(\sin(\theta + \phi) = \sin\theta\cos\phi + \cos\theta\sin\phi = \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) = \dfrac{36}{65} + \dfrac{20}{65} = \dfrac{56}{65}\)  ...(1)

We must also confirm that \(\theta + \phi\) lies in the principal branch \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) of \(\sin^{-1}\). For that, compute

\(\cos(\theta + \phi) = \cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi = \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{13}\right) = \dfrac{48}{65} - \dfrac{15}{65} = \dfrac{33}{65} > 0\).

Since \(\theta + \phi\) is positive with positive cosine, \(0 < \theta + \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore\) from (1), \(\theta + \phi = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{56}{65}\right)\).

\(\therefore \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{13}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{56}{65}\right)\). Hence proved.

stem: The principal solutions of \(cotx = - \sqrt{3}\) are
solution:
**(C)**

\(\cot x = -\sqrt{3}\) if and only if \(\tan x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

We know \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so the reference angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). As the tangent is negative, \(x\) lies in the second or the fourth quadrant.

Using \(\tan(\pi - x) = -\tan x\) and \(\tan(2\pi - x) = -\tan x\):

\(\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) and \(\tan\dfrac{11\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\),

and both \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) lie in \([0,\ 2\pi)\).

\(\therefore\) the principal solutions are \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).

(Options A and D contain \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), where \(\cot x = +\sqrt{3}\); option B's \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) is in the third quadrant, where \(\cot x\) is also \(+\sqrt{3}\).)

stem: Show that: \(\sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{3}{5} \right) + \sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{8}{17} \right) = \sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{77}{85} \right)\).
solution:
Let \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \theta\). Then \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5}\) with \(0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}\).

Let \(\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right) = \phi\). Then \(\sin\phi = \dfrac{8}{17}\) with \(0 < \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\cos\phi = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{64}{289}} = \dfrac{15}{17}\).

Now \(\sin(\theta + \phi) = \sin\theta\cos\phi + \cos\theta\sin\phi = \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{15}{17}\right) + \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right) = \dfrac{45}{85} + \dfrac{32}{85} = \dfrac{77}{85}\)  ...(1)

To place \(\theta + \phi\) inside the principal branch \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) of \(\sin^{-1}\), compute

\(\cos(\theta + \phi) = \cos\theta\cos\phi - \sin\theta\sin\phi = \left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{15}{17}\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right) = \dfrac{60}{85} - \dfrac{24}{85} = \dfrac{36}{85} > 0\).

So \(\theta + \phi\) is positive with positive cosine, i.e. \(0 < \theta + \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore\) from (1), \(\theta + \phi = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{77}{85}\right)\).

\(\therefore \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) + \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{77}{85}\right)\). Hence shown.

subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions and Principal Values
stem: Find the principal value of \(\cot^{- 1}\left( - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)\).
solution:
The principal value of \(\cot^{-1}x\) lies in \((0,\ \pi)\).

Let \(\cot^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \theta\), so \(\cot\theta = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) with \(\theta \in (0,\ \pi)\).

Since \(\cot\theta\) is negative, \(\theta\) lies in the second quadrant. The reference angle is \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), because \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

Using \(\cot(\pi - \theta) = -\cot\theta\):

\(\cot\left(\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), i.e. \(\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), and \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \in (0,\ \pi)\).

\(\therefore\) the principal value of \(\cot^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\) is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

Check directly: \(\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}}{\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}} = \dfrac{-\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

stem: Find the principal solutions of \(cot\theta = 0\).
solution:
\(\cot\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = 0\) requires \(\cos\theta = 0\), with \(\sin\theta \neq 0\) so that \(\cot\theta\) is defined.

The principal solutions are those in \([0,\ 2\pi)\). In that interval \(\cos\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\), and at both of these \(\sin\theta = \pm 1 \neq 0\), so both are admissible.

\(\therefore\) the principal solutions are \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\).

Check: \(\cot\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{0}{1} = 0\) and \(\cot\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = \dfrac{0}{-1} = 0\).

(A common slip is to answer \(0\) and \(\pi\). Those are the angles where \(\tan\theta = 0\), and there \(\cot\theta\) is **undefined**, not zero.)

stem: If \(2\tan^{- 1}(cosx) = \tan^{- 1}(2cosecx)\), then find the value of \(x\).
solution:
For \(|y| < 1\), \(2\tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2y}{1 - y^{2}}\). Taking \(y = \cos x\) (so \(|\cos x| < 1\), i.e. \(\sin x \neq 0\)):

\(2\tan^{-1}(\cos x) = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\cos x}{1 - \cos^{2}x} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\cos x}{\sin^{2}x}\).

Also \(\tan^{-1}(2\,\text{cosec}\,x) = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{\sin x}\).

The given equation therefore becomes

\(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\cos x}{\sin^{2}x} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{\sin x}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{2\cos x}{\sin^{2}x} = \dfrac{2}{\sin x}\)  (as \(\tan^{-1}\) is one-one)

\(\therefore \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin^{2}x} = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}\)

Multiplying by \(\sin^{2}x\) (permissible, \(\sin x \neq 0\)):

\(\therefore \cos x = \sin x\)

\(\therefore \tan x = 1\)

\(\therefore x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Check: at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(\cos x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so L.H.S. \(= 2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\); and \(2\,\text{cosec}\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2\sqrt{2}\), so R.H.S. \(= \tan^{-1}(2\sqrt{2})\). Using the doubling formula, \(\tan\left(2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{2/\sqrt{2}}{1 - 1/2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1/2} = 2\sqrt{2}\), so the two sides agree.

(The full solution set of \(\tan x = 1\) consistent with the equation is \(x = n\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4},\ n \in Z\); \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) is the value asked for.)

stem: Find the general solution of \(sin\theta + sin3\theta + sin5\theta = 0\).
solution:
We have \(\sin\theta + \sin 3\theta + \sin 5\theta = 0\).

Group the first and last terms and use \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\):

\(\therefore (\sin\theta + \sin 5\theta) + \sin 3\theta = 0\)

\(\therefore 2\sin 3\theta\cos 2\theta + \sin 3\theta = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 3\theta\,(2\cos 2\theta + 1) = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 3\theta = 0\) or \(\cos 2\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore \sin 3\theta = 0\) or \(\cos 2\theta = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

The general solution of \(\sin\theta = 0\) is \(\theta = n\pi\), and of \(\cos\theta = \cos\alpha\) is \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha\), \(n \in Z\).

\(\therefore 3\theta = n\pi\) or \(2\theta = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

\(\therefore \theta = \dfrac{n\pi}{3}\) or \(\theta = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), where \(n \in Z\), is the required general solution.

Check: \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) gives \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 0 - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0\).

stem: If \(- 1 \leq x \leq 1\), then prove that \(\sin^{- 1}x + \cos^{- 1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
solution:
Let \(-1 \leq x \leq 1\) and put \(\sin^{-1}x = y\).

By the definition of the principal branch of \(\sin^{-1}\),

\(\sin y = x\) and \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)  ...(1)

Now use the complementary-angle identity \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\right) = \sin y\):

\(\therefore \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\right) = x\)  ...(2)

From (1), multiplying by \(-1\) gives \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq -y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), and adding \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) throughout,

\(0 \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} - y \leq \pi\)  ...(3)

Statement (3) says \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\) lies in \([0,\ \pi]\), which is exactly the principal branch of \(\cos^{-1}\). So (2) and (3) together give

\(\cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}x\).

\(\therefore \sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) for all \(x\) with \(-1 \leq x \leq 1\). Hence proved.

(The restriction \(-1 \leq x \leq 1\) is needed because outside it neither \(\sin^{-1}x\) nor \(\cos^{-1}x\) is defined. Check at \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\); at \(x = -1\): \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \pi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).)

stem: The principle solutions of the equation \(cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\) are _______.
solution:
**(B)**

As \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(0 \leq \dfrac{\pi}{3} < 2\pi\), \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) is a principal solution.

By the allied-angle formula, \(\cos\theta = \cos(2\pi - \theta)\).

\(\therefore \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \cos\left(2\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\), and \(0 \leq \dfrac{5\pi}{3} < 2\pi\).

\(\therefore \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) is also a principal solution.

\(\therefore\) the principal solutions of \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\) are \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\).

(Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants, which rules out options A and D, whose second angles \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) are in the second quadrant; option C's \(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) is in the third.)

stem: Prove that: \(\tan^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) + \tan^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = \frac{\pi}{4}\).
solution:
Here the product of the two arguments is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6} < 1\), so the addition formula \(\tan^{-1}p + \tan^{-1}q = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{p + q}{1 - pq}\right)\) applies directly (no \(\pi\) adjustment is needed).

\(\therefore \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}}{1 - \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3}}\right)\)

\(= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac{5}{6}}{\frac{5}{6}}\right)\)

\(= \tan^{-1}(1)\)

\(= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

\(\therefore \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Hence proved.

stem: Find the general solution of \(\tan^{2}\theta = 1\).
solution:
We have \(\tan^{2}\theta = 1\).

\(\therefore \tan^{2}\theta = \tan^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)  (since \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\))

The general solution of \(\tan^{2}\theta = \tan^{2}\alpha\) is \(\theta = n\pi \pm \alpha\), where \(n \in Z\).

\(\therefore\) with \(\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), the general solution of \(\tan^{2}\theta = 1\) is

\(\theta = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), where \(n \in Z\).

Check: \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) gives \(\tan^{2}\theta = 1\); \(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) gives \((-1)^{2} = 1\); \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\) gives \((-1)^{2} = 1\).

stem: Prove that: \(2\tan^{- 1}\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) + \cos^{- 1}\left( \frac{3}{5} \right) = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
solution:
**Step 1 - convert the first term.**
Since \(\left|\dfrac{1}{3}\right| < 1\), the doubling formula \(2\tan^{-1}y = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2y}{1 - y^{2}}\) applies:

\(2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2 \times \frac{1}{3}}{1 - \frac{1}{9}}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac{2}{3}}{\frac{8}{9}}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)\).

**Step 2 - convert the second term.**
Let \(\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \phi\), so \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{3}{5}\) with \(0 < \phi < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

\(\therefore \sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{9}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}\) and \(\tan\phi = \dfrac{4/5}{3/5} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

\(\therefore \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)\).

**Step 3 - add.**
\(2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) + \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)\).

For \(y > 0\), \(\tan^{-1}y + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{y} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (the two angles are complementary: if \(\tan\alpha = y\) then \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \cot\alpha = \dfrac{1}{y}\), and both angles lie in \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)).

Here \(y = \dfrac{3}{4}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{y} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

\(\therefore 2\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Hence proved.

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\) with the usual notations, prove that \((a - b)^{2}\cos^{2}\left( \frac{C}{2} \right) + (a + b)^{2}\sin^{2}\left( \frac{C}{2} \right) = c^{2}\).
solution:
L.H.S. \(= (a - b)^{2}\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{C}{2}\right) + (a + b)^{2}\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{C}{2}\right)\)

Expand both squares:

\(= (a^{2} - 2ab + b^{2})\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + (a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2})\sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\)

Group the \((a^{2} + b^{2})\) terms and the \(2ab\) terms separately:

\(= (a^{2} + b^{2})\left(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\right) - 2ab\left(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} - \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\right)\)

Now use \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} = 1\) and \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} - \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} = \cos C\):

\(= a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\cos C\)

\(= c^{2}\)  (by the cosine rule, \(\cos C = \dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2} - c^{2}}{2ab}\))

\(=\) R.H.S. Hence proved.

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(a = 13,b = 14,\text{ and }c = 15\), then \(\sin\left( \frac{A}{2} \right)\) = ______.
solution:
**(B)**

\(a = 13,\ b = 14,\ c = 15\), so the semi-perimeter is

\(s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = \dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = \dfrac{42}{2} = 21\)

Half-angle formula:

\(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}}\)

\(s - b = 21 - 14 = 7\), \(s - c = 21 - 15 = 6\), and \(bc = 14 \times 15 = 210\).

\(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7 \times 6}{210}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{42}{210}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\)

which is option (B).

Cross-check by the cosine rule:

\(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc} = \dfrac{196 + 225 - 169}{2 \times 14 \times 15} = \dfrac{252}{420} = \dfrac{3}{5}\)

\(\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \cos A}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{3}{5}}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{5}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{5}\)

so \(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\), the same value by a second route.

Note the trap in the option list: \(\cos A = \dfrac{3}{5}\) gives \(\sin A = \dfrac{4}{5}\), which is option (C). That is \(\sin A\), not \(\sin\dfrac{A}{2}\).

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), prove that \(\sin\left( \frac{B - C}{2} \right) = \frac{(b - c)}{a}\cos\left( \frac{A}{2} \right)\).
solution:
By the sine rule, \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} = 2R\), so \(a = 2R\sin A\), \(b = 2R\sin B\) and \(c = 2R\sin C\).

Start from the ratio on the right-hand side:

\(\dfrac{b - c}{a} = \dfrac{2R\sin B - 2R\sin C}{2R\sin A} = \dfrac{\sin B - \sin C}{\sin A}\)

Apply the sum-to-product identity to the numerator:

\(\sin B - \sin C = 2\cos\left(\dfrac{B + C}{2}\right)\sin\left(\dfrac{B - C}{2}\right)\)

and the double-angle identity to the denominator:

\(\sin A = 2\sin\dfrac{A}{2}\cos\dfrac{A}{2}\)

In \(\triangle ABC\) the angles add to \(\pi\), so \(B + C = \pi - A\), giving \(\dfrac{B + C}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{A}{2}\) and therefore

\(\cos\left(\dfrac{B + C}{2}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \sin\dfrac{A}{2}\)

Substituting both results,

\(\dfrac{b - c}{a} = \dfrac{2\sin\dfrac{A}{2}\ \sin\left(\dfrac{B - C}{2}\right)}{2\sin\dfrac{A}{2}\ \cos\dfrac{A}{2}} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{B - C}{2}\right)}{\cos\dfrac{A}{2}}\)

The cancellation is legitimate because \(0 < A < \pi\) gives \(0 < \dfrac{A}{2} < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} \neq 0\).

Cross-multiplying,

\(\sin\left(\dfrac{B - C}{2}\right) = \dfrac{b - c}{a}\cos\dfrac{A}{2}\)

which is the required identity.

Numerical check with \(a = 13,\ b = 14,\ c = 15\): \(\cos A = \dfrac{3}{5}\) gives \(A = 53.130^{\circ}\); \(\cos B = \dfrac{a^{2} + c^{2} - b^{2}}{2ac} = \dfrac{169 + 225 - 196}{390} = 0.50769\) gives \(B = 59.490^{\circ}\); hence \(C = 67.380^{\circ}\). Left side \(= \sin\left(-3.945^{\circ}\right) = -0.06881\). Right side \(= \dfrac{14 - 15}{13}\cos\left(26.565^{\circ}\right) = -0.076923 \times 0.894427 = -0.06880\). The two sides agree.

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), with usual notations prove that \((a - b)^{2}\cos^{2}\left( \frac{C}{2} \right) + (a + b)^{2}\sin^{2}\left( \frac{C}{2} \right) = c^{2}\).
solution:
L.H.S. \(= (a - b)^{2}\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{C}{2}\right) + (a + b)^{2}\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{C}{2}\right)\)

Expand both squares:

\(= (a^{2} - 2ab + b^{2})\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + (a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2})\sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\)

Collect the \((a^{2} + b^{2})\) terms together and the \(2ab\) terms together:

\(= (a^{2} + b^{2})\left(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\right) - 2ab\left(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} - \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2}\right)\)

Using \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} + \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} = 1\) and \(\cos^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} - \sin^{2}\dfrac{C}{2} = \cos C\),

\(= a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\cos C\)

\(= c^{2}\)  (by the cosine rule)

\(=\) R.H.S. Hence proved.

subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(a = 2,b = 3\) and \(sinA = \frac{2}{3}\), then \(\angle B\) = ?
solution:
**(C)**

By the sine rule, \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B}\).

\(\therefore \dfrac{2}{\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{\sin B}\)

\(\therefore 3 = \dfrac{3}{\sin B}\)

\(\therefore \sin B = 1\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)  (the only angle in \((0, \pi)\) with sine 1).

\(\therefore \angle B = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(a + b + c = 2s\), then prove that \(\sin\left( \frac{A}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\frac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}}\), with usual notations.
solution:
By the cosine rule, \(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc}\).

Also \(\cos A = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2}\), so

\(2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = 1 - \cos A\)

\(\therefore 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc} = \dfrac{2bc - b^{2} - c^{2} + a^{2}}{2bc}\)

The numerator is \(a^{2} - (b^{2} - 2bc + c^{2}) = a^{2} - (b - c)^{2}\), a difference of two squares:

\(\therefore 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{\big(a - (b - c)\big)\big(a + (b - c)\big)}{2bc} = \dfrac{(a - b + c)(a + b - c)}{2bc}\)

Now use \(a + b + c = 2s\):

\(a - b + c = (a + b + c) - 2b = 2s - 2b = 2(s - b)\), and
\(a + b - c = (a + b + c) - 2c = 2s - 2c = 2(s - c)\).

\(\therefore 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{2(s - b) \cdot 2(s - c)}{2bc} = \dfrac{2(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}\)

\(\therefore \sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}\)

Since \(0 < A < \pi\), we have \(0 < \dfrac{A}{2} < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} > 0\) and only the positive square root is admissible.

\(\therefore \sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}}\). Hence proved.

Check on \(a = 13\), \(b = 14\), \(c = 15\): \(s = 21\), so the formula gives \(\sqrt{\dfrac{7 \times 6}{14 \times 15}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\); and directly, \(\cos A = \dfrac{196 + 225 - 169}{2(14)(15)} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1 - 3/5}{2} = \dfrac{1}{5}\). They agree.

subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} = ac\), then \(\angle B\) = ?
solution:
**(B)**

The stem as printed reads \(c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} = ac\), a double equality no triangle can satisfy — see the errata note. The question is answered on the intended condition \(c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2} = ac\), which is how the same question is printed in the March 2023 paper and how the Balbharati textbook carries it.

By the cosine rule,

\(\cos B = \dfrac{c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}}{2ac}\)

Substituting the given condition \(c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2} = ac\):

\(\cos B = \dfrac{ac}{2ac} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

Since \(0 < B < \pi\), the only such angle is

\(B = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)

which is option (B).

subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2} = ac\), then \(\angle B\) = ______.
solution:
**(B)**

By the cosine rule, \(\cos B = \dfrac{c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}}{2ac}\).

The given condition is \(c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2} = ac\), which is exactly the numerator.

\(\therefore \cos B = \dfrac{ac}{2ac} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)  (the only angle in \((0, \pi)\) with cosine \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)).

\(\therefore \angle B = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

(As a sanity check, options A, C and D would need \(\cos B = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(0\) and \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), i.e. \(c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}\) equal to \(\sqrt{2}\,ac\), \(0\) and \(\sqrt{3}\,ac\) respectively.)

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), if \(a = 18,b = 24\text{ and }c = 30\) then find the value of \(\sin\left( \frac{A}{2} \right)\).
solution:
Here \(a = 18\), \(b = 24\), \(c = 30\).

\(s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = \dfrac{18 + 24 + 30}{2} = 36\).

\(\therefore s - b = 36 - 24 = 12\) and \(s - c = 36 - 30 = 6\).

By the half-angle formula,

\(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}}\)

\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{12 \times 6}{24 \times 30}}\)

\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{72}{720}}\)

\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{10}}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\).

Check: \(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc} = \dfrac{576 + 900 - 324}{2(24)(30)} = \dfrac{1152}{1440} = \dfrac{4}{5}\), and \(\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1 - \cos A}{2} = \dfrac{1 - 4/5}{2} = \dfrac{1}{10}\), which agrees.

\(\therefore \sin\left(\dfrac{A}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\).

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), prove that: \(\frac{cosA}{a} + \frac{cosB}{b} + \frac{cosC}{c} = \frac{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}{2abc}\).
solution:
By the cosine rule,

\(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc}\), so dividing by \(a\),  \(\dfrac{\cos A}{a} = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2abc}\).

Similarly,

\(\dfrac{\cos B}{b} = \dfrac{c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}}{2abc}\)  and  \(\dfrac{\cos C}{c} = \dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2} - c^{2}}{2abc}\).

Notice that all three now have the same denominator \(2abc\). Adding,

L.H.S. \(= \dfrac{\cos A}{a} + \dfrac{\cos B}{b} + \dfrac{\cos C}{c} = \dfrac{(b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}) + (c^{2} + a^{2} - b^{2}) + (a^{2} + b^{2} - c^{2})}{2abc}\)

In the numerator each of \(a^{2}\), \(b^{2}\) and \(c^{2}\) appears twice with a \(+\) sign and once with a \(-\) sign, so the numerator is \(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}\).

\(= \dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}{2abc} = \) R.H.S. Hence proved.

subtopic: Solution of Triangle — Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\), \((a + b)cosC + (b + c)cosA + (c + a)cosB\) is equal to _______.
solution:
**(C)**

L.H.S. \(= (a + b)\cos C + (b + c)\cos A + (c + a)\cos B\)

Multiply out every bracket:

\(= (a\cos C + b\cos C) + (b\cos A + c\cos A) + (c\cos B + a\cos B)\)

Regroup the six terms into projection-rule pairs:

\(= (a\cos C + c\cos A) + (b\cos A + a\cos B) + (c\cos B + b\cos C)\)

By the projection rule, \(a\cos C + c\cos A = b\), \(b\cos A + a\cos B = c\) and \(c\cos B + b\cos C = a\).

\(= b + c + a\)

\(= a + b + c\).

subtopic: Applications of Sine, Cosine and Projection Rules
stem: In \(\bigtriangleup ABC\) if \(a = 13,b = 14,c = 15\) then find the values of (i) \(secA\) (ii) \(\csc\frac{A}{2}\).
solution:
Here \(a = 13\), \(b = 14\), \(c = 15\).

\(s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2} = \dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21\).

\(\therefore s - a = 8\), \(s - b = 7\), \(s - c = 6\).

**(i) \(\sec A\).**
By the cosine rule,

\(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc} = \dfrac{14^{2} + 15^{2} - 13^{2}}{2(14)(15)} = \dfrac{196 + 225 - 169}{420} = \dfrac{252}{420} = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

\(\therefore \sec A = \dfrac{1}{\cos A} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).

**(ii) \(\text{cosec}\dfrac{A}{2}\).**
By the half-angle formula,

\(\sin\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(s - b)(s - c)}{bc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7 \times 6}{14 \times 15}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{42}{210}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\).

\(\therefore \text{cosec}\dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{A}{2}} = \sqrt{5}\).

Check that the two parts agree: \(\cos A = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\dfrac{A}{2} = 1 - 2\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = \dfrac{3}{5}\), which is the value found in (i).

\(\therefore \sec A = \dfrac{5}{3}\) and \(\text{cosec}\dfrac{A}{2} = \sqrt{5}\).

stem: Find the general solution of \(sin2x + sin4x + sin6x = 0\).
solution:
We have \(\sin 2x + \sin 4x + \sin 6x = 0\).

Group the first and last terms (the ones equidistant from \(4x\)) and use \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\):

\(\therefore (\sin 2x + \sin 6x) + \sin 4x = 0\)

\(\therefore 2\sin 4x\cos 2x + \sin 4x = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 4x\,(2\cos 2x + 1) = 0\)

\(\therefore \sin 4x = 0\) or \(\cos 2x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore \sin 4x = 0\) or \(\cos 2x = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

The general solution of \(\sin\theta = 0\) is \(\theta = n\pi\), and of \(\cos\theta = \cos\alpha\) is \(\theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha\), \(n \in Z\).

\(\therefore 4x = n\pi\) or \(2x = 2n\pi \pm \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\)

\(\therefore x = \dfrac{n\pi}{4}\) or \(x = n\pi \pm \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), where \(n \in Z\), is the required general solution.

Check: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) gives \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \sin\pi + \sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} = 1 + 0 - 1 = 0\); \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) gives \(\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3} + \sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} + \sin 2\pi = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 0 = 0\).
